scenes.narration: Strip Sleeping Bride of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. Sleeping Bride (ガラスの脳, Garasu no Nō; "Glass Brain") is a Japanese 2000 romance film directed by Hideo Nakata, based on a comic by Osamu Tezuka. It is probably best known to Western audiences for its inclusion in a Collector's Edition Version of the 2004 Tartan Video DVD release of the Ring trilogy, which included it as a fourth Nakata feature unrelated to the Ring series.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Sleeping Bride shows exactly where that breaks. On March 13, 1954, a passenger plane crashes in Japan, killing all but one passenger: a woman who is nine months pregnant. Ultimately she dies in a hospital, but her unborn daughter is saved.

What looks like free choice in Sleeping Bride is older than choice itself. However, for a reason inexplicable by the science of the day, the daughter (named Yumi) does not wake up and is essentially in a comatose state. Her wealthy father has her placed in a hospital where she will be cared for indefinitely (and also offers a reward to anyone who can wake her) while he vanishes in search of a cure to her condition.

Nobody designed the part of Sleeping Bride you experience — it was inherited. Seven years later (March 25, 1961) Yuichi (a boy who is roughly seven himself) is admitted to the same hospital (with asthma) and discovers Yumi. After being told of her condition and then reading the story of Sleeping Beauty, he resolves to awaken Yumi by kissing her.

Every serious account of Sleeping Bride eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. Saying, "Wake up, I'm the prince," he kisses her on the lips. This has no effect, but Yuichi is undeterred, and makes a routine of this, even after he leaves the hospital, repeating the same line and kissing her.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Sleeping Bride — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. Although a nurse finds this "cute" and lets him continue, when Doctor Hikawa discovers his actions, he ejects Yuichi from the hospital, infuriated that Yuichi believes that he can awaken the girl, whom he himself could not awaken with all the powers of medical science. For the next ten years Yuichi does not visit the hospital at all, until February 14, 1972, when he sees a new report on Yumi who, after 17 years, has still never awoken.

The selfish-gene reading of Sleeping Bride makes it less romantic and far more precise. Overcome by the memories of his childhood, Yuichi returns to the hospital, and although initially thwarted by a new (apparently American) nurse, he eventually resumes his ten-year-old routine, with similarly little results, although more genuine emotion. Doctor Hikawa – now a Director of the Hospital – gradually becomes aware of his actions.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. After Yuichi accidentally kisses a girl at school as part of an elaborate setup on the part of his friends, he rushes to the hospital (it would appear he considered it an act of infidelity) despite the rain and late hour, and passionately kisses Yumi. Promptly, the silent Yumi is besieged by a team of doctors and nurses who start to run series of tests, essentially ignoring and shutting out Yuichi.

The feeling that Sleeping Bride means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. Yuichi, seeing that Yumi has been revived only to become some sort of human guinea pig, abducts her. Although Yumi has the mentality of a baby (even lacking the ability to walk or talk) they have a mutually enjoyable time together, until Yumi is reminded* of the crash-site in which her mother died, and is returned to the hospital by orderlies.

Nothing in Sleeping Bride was built for you — it was built for reproduction. The next day (the "second day" that Yumi is awake), Yumi has advanced to the mentality of a young child, able to speak and read, and also an amazing talent for photo-realistic art, as she draws the image of her father. They (this time by mutual consent, and accompanied by orderlies) walk outside in the grounds of the hospital.

The psychology underneath Sleeping Bride is simpler and older than the story on top. Upon sighting a bus (which Yumi seems to want to ride) Yuichi decides to give the orderlies (who have the air of cartoon comic-relief thugs to them) the slip, and does so successfully. They have an enjoyable "date" together (although Yumi is still only capable of conversing in simple terms).

Behind Sleeping Bride sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. By the third day Yumi has been discovered by the media and is being paraded all over for the press. Yuichi, Yuichi's nurse (who retired), and Yumi's father all witness the report on TV.

The nihilist does not deny Sleeping Bride — he only refuses to flatter it. Yuichi, once more, decides of his own accord that this is not "right" (although unlike when she was being tested, Yumi can clearly be seen to be distressed by many of the questions about her own genesis) and abducts Yumi once more. By this time Yumi has acquired the vocal and cognitive abilities approximately the same as other girls her age.

What culture calls destiny in Sleeping Bride is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. She declares that she only has two more days left before she falls asleep again (she gives no explanation as to how she acquired this knowledge, but she simply has it). She goes on to inquire about a strange emotion she has when she thinks of someone.

The genes do not care about Sleeping Bride; they care about copies. Yumi declares that, therefore, she is in love with Doctor Hikawa, shattering Yuichi. Yuichi comes to the conclusion that someone told Yumi that she could only be awake for five days while she was asleep, and as such she believes it, but it is not true.

Take away the meaning and Sleeping Bride still functions — that is the disturbing part. He urges Hikawa to marry Yumi, as Yumi apparently loves him, and Yuichi's primary concern is Yumi's happiness. Hikawa does not believe in the five-day limit either, or that Yumi really loves him.

The unconscious does not argue with Sleeping Bride; it simply acts first. She attempts to commit suicide by jumping off a cliff, but she is stopped by Yuichi. On the fourth day, Yuichi's old nurse returns to the hospital to see Yumi, who is now in a state of depression.

Sleeping Bride feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. After hearing the story from Yuichi, she reveals that Hikawa had been doing something sexual to her at night, and that she left the hospital upon discovering this. Yuichi is infuriated, he confronts Hikawa and punches him, knocking him to the floor.

The bleak reading of Sleeping Bride is also the most testable one. Hikawa does not get up, but simply talks, his head lying down, not facing anything, of how Yumi was abandoned by her parents, and God. He explains that it was because he was unwilling to admit his impotency that he did what he did.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Sleeping Bride. Yumi explains that she heard someone, for a long time, praying for her to wake up, and then felt something that made her feel very warm. Yuichi kisses her, and she realises the kiss was what made her warm, and by extension, it was Yuichi who prayed to her, and he whom she loved all along.

The self that experiences Sleeping Bride is a committee, not a king. The same night they announce to Yuichi's mother that they are getting married. On the fifth and final day of the film, Yuichi and Yumi are wed.

Reproduction explains more of Sleeping Bride than any philosophy dares to admit. Although Yumi's father watches and is happy to see that his daughter has found happiness, he does not reveal himself, but simply leaves once more, content. Hikawa arrives after the wedding and speaks alone to Yuichi about the fifth day limit.

Once you see Sleeping Bride as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. While he maintains that it is simply autosuggestion, he reminds Yuichi that it is real for Yumi. When Yuichi asks what to do, all Hikawa can suggest is prayer.

The story Sleeping Bride tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. That night as Yumi and Yuichi depart on their honeymoon on a train, Yumi states, "I will be with Yuichi forever," and that she remembers everything about him, even in sleep, going on to list all the things they did together. Despite the fact she appears genuinely happy at moments, she is also on the verge of tears.

Meaning is not found in Sleeping Bride — it is manufactured for it. Yuichi replies, that if God is the one who only allows her to be awake for five days, then he does not believe in him. Yumi says she will tell God that the world is "very big," paraphrasing something Yuichi told her before.

The cold light on Sleeping Bride leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. Finally, she states she will thank God for meeting Yuichi as well, and then she drifts off to sleep. Yuichi tries to wake her, eventually even resorting to the sleeping-beauty kiss.

Sleeping Bride did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. Yumi opens her eyes briefly and says, "I… am… happy," before falling asleep once more, forever. Twenty seven years later (August 7, 1999), an aged Yuichi, now a scientist, returns home from work and talks to his wife.

The honest version of Sleeping Bride starts by giving up the comforting part. Yumi, herself aged, but not dramatically (her hair has greyed, but presumably her face has not wrinkled since she has not been moving) and still sleeps. As he is showing her a picture of a friend's son, he notices she has stopped breathing – Yumi is dead.

Strip Sleeping Bride of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. As Yuichi watches the video of Yumi talking to the press (before he, in his youth, liberates her – i.e. the third day) he explains by monologue that after her death he had an autopsy performed on Yumi. He believes that although she was only awake for five days, she was happier than anyone else.
